whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Strategy Designer exam?

personas.label: UX and service design practitioners
personas.description: You research users and shape service experiences on Salesforce projects, and want a credential for that work.

personas.label: Discovery workshop consultants
personas.description: You work with clients to understand their needs and turn findings into a practical solution direction.

personas.label: Product owners connecting users and business
personas.description: You balance user needs with business outcomes and help teams choose what to tackle first.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Strategy Designer exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This is a mid-level exam about design practice rather than Salesforce features. It checks how you learn about users, define the real problem, guide workshops, and connect design choices to business outcomes. Admins and developers may find the research methods less familiar.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
70% to pass, which is 42 correct answers out of 60.
Design methods. Expect research, synthesis, problem framing, facilitation, and outcome measurement.
Project judgement. Many items ask for the best next step in a situation rather than a product feature.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Hands-on discovery and research experience helps. Because the pass threshold is higher than many exams, target at least 80% on practice sets before booking.

examFormat.heading: What to expect on the Strategy Designer exam
examFormat.intro: You may sit the proctored exam online or at a test centre. The questions commonly cover these situations:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many items place you in a project situation: a vague request, stakeholders who disagree, or research that challenges the original brief. You must choose the designer’s next move.
bestWayToPass: Choose research methods: Know when interviews, observation, surveys, or analytics answer the question.
Make sense of findings: Practise affinity mapping, personas, journey maps, and service blueprints.
Define the problem: Turn evidence into a clear problem statement and useful How Might We questions.
Connect design to outcomes: Tie decisions to business goals and measurable results.

certificationCard.description: This credential covers how to set the direction for a Salesforce solution through research, problem framing, facilitation, and business value. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 70% pass mark, weighted towards Value Design (32%) and Intangible Deliverables (26%).

keyConcepts.h2: Strategy Designer exam concepts to know

blocks.heading: Start with people and evidence
blocks.body: Human-centred design begins with the people who will use the solution. Learn their goals, tasks, and frustrations before proposing features. Interviews and contextual observation can explain why people behave a certain way; surveys and usage data can show how common a pattern is. Set a research objective, recruit people who represent the users, and use neutral questions.

blocks.heading: Turn findings into a service picture
blocks.body: Synthesis helps the team find meaning in research. Affinity maps cluster observations into themes; personas describe user needs; journey maps show steps, feelings, and pain points. A service blueprint adds the staff, systems, and processes that support each step. Together, these tools reveal the wider experience beyond a single screen.

blocks.heading: Show the business value
blocks.body: A design proposal should support a business goal, such as resolving cases faster or improving conversion, with an agreed way to measure success. Identify stakeholders and what matters to them. Compare value with effort to decide what to address first. An experience vision gives the team a common direction and explains why it matters.

blocks.heading: Explore and deliver in agile
blocks.body: Design is part of agile delivery. A design sprint takes a team from a defined problem to a tested prototype in a short period. In dual-track agile, discovery explores and tests ideas while delivery builds work that has been validated. Prototypes may be sketches or clickable models; early user feedback is cheaper to act on than feedback after software is built.

blocks.heading: Design with care and inclusion
blocks.body: Consider who could be excluded or harmed by a design. Include people with different needs and abilities, and follow accessibility standards. Explain how you collect and use data, and avoid research bias such as speaking only with easy-to-reach users. For AI features, plan for transparency, trust, human oversight, and errors.

scenarioTips.h2: Ways to prepare for the Strategy Designer exam
scenarioTips.intro: When a question asks what to do next, look for the step that improves understanding of the problem before the team commits to a solution.

blocks.heading: Use the design thinking cycle
blocks.body: Understand, define, ideate, prototype, and test. The process can loop back; new evidence may call for more research.

blocks.heading: Match the method to the question
blocks.body: Use interviews and observation to learn why. Use surveys and analytics to measure how many. Select the method that fits the information needed.

blocks.heading: Map the whole journey
blocks.body: Show user steps, emotions, and pain points. Add a service blueprint to reveal the people and systems supporting each step.

blocks.heading: Frame an open problem
blocks.body: Write a problem statement grounded in findings, then ask How Might We questions that invite ideas without prescribing a fix.

blocks.heading: Make workshops inclusive
blocks.body: Set a clear goal and activities, make room for every participant, then close with decisions and owners for next steps.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for designers
nextCertsAfter.intro: Build on your strategy design knowledge with these related Salesforce credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: A client asks for a dashboard, saying sales staff are missing quota. What should the designer do before choosing a solution?
options: Ask developers which dashboard is quickest to build
Create the requested dashboard immediately
Investigate why sales staff are missing quota
Reuse a dashboard from another client
sampleQuestions.explanation: The dashboard is a proposed fix. Research the cause first to see whether a dashboard would address the underlying issue.
whyWrong: Build effort does not establish what users need.
Starting with the proposed fix may solve the wrong issue.
Another client’s needs and context may differ.

sampleQuestions.question: A team wants to learn why service agents move between several screens during calls. Which research approach is most useful?
options: Review the organization’s user license count
Compare a competitor’s product
Observe agents doing their work
Send a broad online survey
sampleQuestions.explanation: Watching agents in their normal setting can reveal the steps they take and why.
whyWrong: License totals do not explain how agents work.
Competitor research cannot show what causes this team’s behavior.
A survey can measure frequency but may miss the detail behind the behavior.

sampleQuestions.question: The team has completed 15 interviews and collected many notes. What should it do next?
options: Cluster the notes into themes with affinity mapping
Build a feature based on the first note
Remove findings that do not support the original brief
Schedule 15 more interviews before reviewing the notes
sampleQuestions.explanation: Affinity mapping helps the team organize individual observations into patterns it can discuss.
whyWrong: One note may not represent the broader evidence.
Discarding conflicting findings introduces bias.
More research before synthesis adds data without making sense of what is already known.

sampleQuestions.question: Which artefact records a customer’s steps, feelings, and difficulties during an experience?
options: A data model diagram
A journey map
A release calendar
A test plan
sampleQuestions.explanation: A journey map lays out the stages of an experience and can show emotions and pain points at each stage.
whyWrong: A data model describes data entities and relationships.
A release calendar shows planned delivery dates.
A test plan lists checks to perform.

sampleQuestions.question: The team needs to show customer steps as well as the staff, systems, and processes supporting them. Which artefact fits?
options: A service blueprint
A collection of visual style references
A persona
A wireframe
sampleQuestions.explanation: A service blueprint maps the customer experience and the behind-the-scenes work that supports it.
whyWrong: A mood board communicates visual direction.
A persona summarizes a user type and its needs.
A wireframe outlines a screen, not the service behind it.

sampleQuestions.question: Which prompt is the strongest How Might We question?
options: Why do agents take so long to complete this work?
How might we help new agents find answers on their own?
How might we create a new Lightning page for this process?
Should we add three fields to the current case layout?
sampleQuestions.explanation: This question describes a user need while leaving room for several possible solutions.
whyWrong: This wording blames users instead of opening up exploration.
This prompt already chooses a particular implementation.
This yes-or-no question asks about a specific change.

sampleQuestions.question: Two senior stakeholders have different priorities for the project. What is the best next step for the designer?
options: Let the stakeholder with the strongest opinion choose the direction
Bring both stakeholders together to review shared goals and research
Build both proposals so neither stakeholder has to compromise
Make the decision alone and inform both stakeholders afterward
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shared goals and evidence give stakeholders a basis for reaching a supported decision.
whyWrong: The loudest opinion may not reflect user needs or project goals.
Building both can waste time before a direction is agreed.
A decision made without stakeholders can lose their support.

sampleQuestions.question: The team has 20 ideas but can pursue only five. How should it select them?
options: Choose the ideas with the most technical complexity
Take the first five suggestions
Pick the ideas the team finds most entertaining
Compare user and business value with the effort required
sampleQuestions.explanation: Comparing value and effort helps the team focus on ideas with a worthwhile return.
whyWrong: Complexity alone does not show whether an idea is useful.
The order ideas were suggested is not a meaningful selection method.
Enjoyment does not establish value for users or the business.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants agent feedback on a new case flow next week, before development begins. What should it prepare?
options: Release notes
A complete production version
A simple prototype for agents to try
A lengthy specification document
sampleQuestions.explanation: A small prototype lets the team test the idea with users before investing in a full build.
whyWrong: Release notes describe changes after they are made.
A production build is costly to change if testing reveals problems.
A document does not let agents try the interaction.

sampleQuestions.question: In dual-track agile, what is the discovery track responsible for?
options: Exploring and testing ideas so delivery can build validated work
Set business-linked measures before launch, then track them
Writing all production code
Providing ongoing production support
sampleQuestions.explanation: Discovery runs alongside delivery and tests ideas before the team builds them.
whyWrong: Discovery continues during delivery rather than waiting until the end.
Implementation work belongs to the delivery track.
Production support is a separate responsibility.

sampleQuestions.question: How can a team assess whether a redesign delivered value?
options: Ask each project member whether they like the new design
Include field workers in research to learn their needs
Record how long the project took
Count how many screens were added
sampleQuestions.explanation: Measures tied to goals and defined before release show whether the change had the intended effect.
whyWrong: Team preference alone does not measure impact.
Project duration does not show whether business outcomes improved.
The number of screens does not indicate value.

sampleQuestions.question: Research included office staff, but field workers will also use the solution. What concern should the team address?
options: There is no concern because both groups work for the company
Including field workers will only increase project cost
The design may miss field workers’ needs if they are not included
Field workers can be expected to adapt to any design
sampleQuestions.explanation: Leaving out a user group can produce a solution that does not fit its work or environment.
whyWrong: The missing group creates a risk that should be explored.
The question is about representation and fit, not simply research cost.
Assuming users will adapt does not establish that the design works for them.

sampleQuestions.question: What does an experience vision provide to a project team?
options: Replace research with a single statement of the intended design
List every field that will appear on each page in the final product
Set the amount of money available for the project
Give the team a common picture of the intended future experience
sampleQuestions.explanation: The vision aligns the team and stakeholders on the direction and reason for the work.
whyWrong: A vision should be informed by research, not replace it.
A page-by-page field list is implementation detail.
Budget planning is a separate activity.

sampleQuestions.question: In a 12-person workshop, two participants dominate the discussion. What should the facilitator try?
options: Use a structured activity so every participant can contribute ideas
Ask the quieter participants to leave the meeting
Let the same two participants continue to lead the discussion
End the workshop early instead of continuing the conversation
sampleQuestions.explanation: Structured participation gives each person time to contribute and reduces the effect of dominant voices.
whyWrong: Removing participants reduces inclusion rather than improving it.
Continuing unchanged prevents other perspectives from being heard.
Ending early wastes the opportunity to make progress together.

sampleQuestions.question: A proposed AI feature will suggest replies to customers. What should the designer plan for?
options: No review is needed because AI responses are always correct
Only the speed of the feature
Only the color of the suggestion panel
Plan for trust, transparency, and AI mistakes
sampleQuestions.explanation: Responsible AI design makes the feature understandable, provides appropriate oversight, and accounts for mistakes.
whyWrong: AI can make errors, so a plan for handling them is needed.
Performance matters but does not cover trust or error handling.
Visual styling does not address the key risks of AI suggestions.
